intervention.description: systematic investigation of tensile creep behavior

structure.description: dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels; dislocation jogging and tangling configurations; dynamic precipitates identified as M23C6 or a Cr-rich σ phase along grain boundaries

evidence_units.mechanism: creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion; abnormally high stress exponents in HSR ascribed to the coordinative contributions of dynamic recrystallization and dynamic precipitation; barriers imposed by precipitates and severe initial deformation referred to as factors to increase the activation energy for creep deformation

outcome.measurement_method: stress exponent and activation energy analysis from creep data

evidence_spans: The tensile creep behavior of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy was systematically investigated over an intermediate temperature range (500–600 °C) and applied stress (140–400 MPa).
The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II).
The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol −1 , whereas the HSR showed much higher corresponding values of 8.9–14 and 380 kJ mol −1 .
Microstructural examinations on the deformed samples revealed remarkable dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels.
Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively.
Moreover, dynamic precipitates identified as M 23 C 6 or a Cr-rich σ phase were formed along grain boundaries in HSR.

The diffusion-compensated strain rate versus modulus-compensated stress data analysis implied that the creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion.
Nevertheless, the abnormally high stress exponents in HSR were ascribed to the coordinative contributions of dynamic recrystallization and dynamic precipitation.
Simultaneously, the barriers imposed by these precipitates and severe initial deformation were referred to so as to increase the activation energy for creep deformation.

evidence_units.mechanism: Dislocation-climb mechanism operative in LSR, consistent with activation energy comparable to lattice diffusion

outcome.measurement_method: Arrhenius plot of steady-state creep rate vs reciprocal temperature

comparison.direction: slightly lower than lattice diffusion range

evidence_spans: In the low-stress region (subsequently denoted as LSR-region I), the stress exponent values vary in the range of 5 to 6, and the average activation energy Q takes a value of 268 kJ mol −1 .

It should be noted that the average activation energy of 268 kJ mol −1 in LSR-region I is only slightly lower than the range of activation energies for lattice diffusion of the constituent elements in the alloy (288–317 kJ mol −1 [ [17] ]), and thus can be considered to be comparable to the lattice diffusion of the constituent elements in the alloy.
The two characteristic parameters suggest a dislocation-climb mechanism operative in LSR.

After being deformed at 500 °C/200 MPa (LSR), only a few short straight dislocation segments were displayed inside the grains ( Figure 7 a), and in particular, several lath-shaped areas were formed with closely-spaced dislocations arranged ( Figure 7 b).

intervention.description: Fracture analysis of crept samples in HSR

structure.description: Ductile transgranular fracture with dimples and slip striations

evidence_units.mechanism: Dislocation interactions during high-temperature deformation contributing to vacancy generation and void nucleation, leading to ductile failure despite precipitate presence

comparison.baseline_state: brittle failure at grain boundaries due to precipitates

evidence_spans: All the fractographs in Figure 10 for HSR from 500 °C to 600 °C exhibit typical ductile rupture, where both the width and depth of dimples increase with temperature.
The ductile creep failure may be associated with the dislocation interactions during high-temperature deformation, which contribute to the progressive generation of vacancies and nucleation of voids.

evidence_units.mechanism: stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion
evidence_spans: The observed jog configurations are indicative of a dislocation climb process, and thus the stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion may be the operative creep mechanism of the present high-entropy alloy in LSR.
At low stresses, the values were approximately 5 to 6 and 268 kJ/mol
Stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion is suggested as a possible rate-dominating mechanism at low stresses.

evidence_spans: creep deformation in HSR exhibits abnormally high stress exponents of 8.9–14 and an average activation energy of 380 kJ mol −1 .
At high-stress regions, the corresponding values were 8.9–14 and 380 kJ/mol.
At high stresses, obvious dynamic recrystallization occurred, leading to the refinement of average grain size.
Simultaneously, nano-sized M 23 C 6 carbides and the Cr-rich tetragonal σ phase were dynamically precipitated.
High density of tangled and curved dislocation substructures was observed.
The anomalously high stress exponent and activation energy in HSR were attributed to the combinative effects of dynamic recrystallization and precipitation.
In particular, the precipitates act as barriers for dislocation motion via producing boundary obstacle stress, resulting in high activation energy for creep deformation.
However, lattice-diffusion controlled dislocation climb is still responsible for the deformation mechanism in HSR.
